THE SHANGHAI TIMES, FRIDAY, AUGUST 23481
LAND TAX PAYMENT
BY COERCION
If anything were needed to illustrate
the difficulties of administration in
Shanghai it would be the fact that the
Council had to barricade up the entrances
to houses in lanes on Ferry Road in order
to get the landlords to pay the Land Tax.
In any other community, the Council of
the city or county would merely have
taken the defaulters to Court and have
obtained judgment against them — a
judgment which would have been ex-
ecuted by the Court in the ordinary way
if it had not been promptly met by the
defaulters themselves. But here in
Shanghai, where the Land Tax is given
ratepayers' approval just like the General
Municipal Rate and where the Council
has the clearest of legal title to collect,
it was apparently found necessary to take
direct coercive action as against what
would have been an ordinary process of
law elsewhere. This is the most unsatis-
factory feature of the incident, reported
elsewhere in this issue, in which the
Council acted suddenly at midnight of 863
Wednesday and erected barricades block- 837
ing the entrance to a terrace of houses
in Ferry Road and also took similar action
regarding property in the Eastern District.
There was no question of the non-
payment of Land Tax in respect of pro-
perty which has not been registered.
It ought to be explained that in the
early days of the Settlement foreigners
could acquire land from Chinese and have
that land registered at their respective
Consulates. All such registered land
became subject to the Land Tax, and a
considerable quantity of Chinese-owned
land was also registered in foreign
names for the sake of the better protection
and clearer legal title attached to such
registration. By far the larger proportion
of all land in the Settlement has been
registered for years and upon such land
the Land Tax has been duly paid. But
about one-sixth of the total land in the
Settlement remains unregistered and it
is upon this that owners have been re-
fusing to pay, this representing a serious
loss every year to the Council on what
it should be able to count for certain as
being normal revenue. The Council has
now rightly taken the view that property
upon which no Land Tax is paid cannot
expect to continue to enjoy the amenities
of municipal roads, and that the Council
is justified in cutting off such property
from having access to such roads. That
in the case of the property on Ferry Road
the Council's action had such a swift
response by the payment of the taxes
yesterday morning shows that in the
minds of the owners there was never any
doubt as to their legal liability.
Regarding the tenants of the barricad-
ed property—tenants who have doubtless
paid their rates in the ordinary way—one
can sympathize with them in any sense
of grievance they might have had,
although the Council in no way interfered
with such essential residential services
as water, light, etc. Those who ordered
action on behalf of the Council doubtless
had the position of the tenants closely in
mind, for the question was raised in the
case of the former Yu Yuen Road bar-
ricades incident as to whether a tenant
who paid an inclusive rental would not
have redress against the Council if
occupational benefits were denied him in
the process of coercive action against
another person. Points such as these,
of course, are merely incidental to the
case under review. The main fact is that
owners of unregistered land have an
obligation to pay the Land Tax to the
Council and that the Council can take
action against them if they do not pay.
The pity of it is, to our mind, that that
action needs to be outside an ordinary
Court. It is an extremely serious matter
for this Settlement when its administra-
tive body is deprived or sceptical of re-
course to simple legal machinery for the
enforcement of its clear revenue rights
and is forced to take punitive action of
physical character.

《字林西报》，星期五，1937年8月[日期OCR不清，原文为23481]
以强制手段
缴付地税
若需举例说明上海行政管理的困难，事实莫过于工部局不得不封锁渡轮路（Ferry Road）弄堂内房屋的入口，以迫使房东缴纳地税。在任何其他社区，市或县议会只需将违约者诉诸法庭并获得判决——如果违约者不主动履行，法庭便会按常规执行该判决。但在上海，地税如同一般市政捐税一样需经纳税人批准，且工部局拥有最明确的合法征收权，却显然发现有必要采取直接强制措施，而这在其他地方本可通过正常的法律程序解决。这是本次事件中最令人不满之处，本期其他版面亦有报道；工部局于[日期OCR不清，原文为863]星期三午夜突然行动，竖起路障封锁了渡轮路一排房屋的入口，并对东区物业采取了类似行动。
此处不涉及未登记物业的地税欠缴问题。需要说明的是，在租界早期，外国人可以从中国人手中购买土地，并在各自领事馆进行登记。所有此类已登记土地均需缴纳地税，且为了获得更好的保护和更清晰的法定产权，大量华人拥有的土地也以外国人名义进行了登记。租界内绝大部分土地多年来均已登记，其地税也已按时缴纳。但租界内约六分之一的土地仍未登记，业主一直拒绝为此缴税，这导致工部局每年在本应确认为正常收入的项目上遭受严重损失。工部局现在正确地认为，不缴纳地税的物业无权继续享受市政道路提供的便利，工部局有权切断此类物业使用这些道路的通道。就渡轮路物业而言，工部局的行动迅速得到了回应，业主于昨晨缴清了税款，这表明业主心中对其法律责任从未有过任何怀疑。
关于被封锁物业的租户——这些租户无疑已按常规缴纳了捐税——对于他们可能产生的任何委屈感，人们可以表示同情，尽管工部局并未干扰供水、供电等必要的居住服务。代表工部局下令采取行动的人无疑密切考虑到了租户的处境，因为在先前愚园路（Yu Yuen Road）路障事件中曾提出这样一个问题：如果在针对他人的强制行动过程中，租户被剥夺了居住权益，那么支付全包租金的租户是否无法向工部局寻求救济。当然，这类问题仅是本案的附带事项。主要事实是，未登记土地的业主有义务向工部局缴纳地税，若其不缴纳，工部局可对其采取行动。令我们感到遗憾的是，这种行动需要在普通法庭之外进行。当这一租界的行政机构被剥夺或对诉诸简单法律机制以强制执行其明确的税收权利持怀疑态度，并被迫采取具有物理性质的惩罚性行动时，这对本租界而言是一个极其严重的问题。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, THURSDAY, AUGUST 5, 1937

S.M.C. Barriers
Exclude Houses
From Ferry Road

Council Strikes Suddenly
at Midnight

UTMOST SECRECY

Yu Yuen Rd. Tax Incident
Recalled by Move

Striking swiftly at midnight last night, agents of the Shanghai Municipal Council blocked off a terrace of houses at Lane 427 in Ferry Road with boards surmounted with barbed wire. Moving quietly from the Gordon Road Police Station, the squad of P.W.D. coolies reached the lane and completed the job within twenty minutes, quickly and efficiently.

The unexpected move by the S.M.C. was almost exactly similar to the creating of a "Forbidden City" in Yu Yuen Road on March 11 of this year when the same body isolated a block of houses which had failed to pay taxes.

The entire move last night was done with an obvious attempt to preserve the utmost secrecy. Aside from agents of the S.M.C., several foreign police officers, Chinese constables, and about twenty P.W.D. coolies, the only spectators of the scene were representatives of the "North-China Daily News."

Unlike the blockading last March, the affair last night was done with no commotion or friction whatever, partly perhaps because the houses attended to were in the International Settlement instead of Chinese territory.

Careful Arrangements

It was apparent that careful arrangements had been made in advance for the two entrances to the lane of houses were blocked with barricades that fitted perfectly. Each entrance to the terrace was off a lane, the lanes being about 100 yards apart. When one job was completed, the small detachment moved down the street to the other entrance. Here, the work was delayed for a few minutes owing to a miscalculation. The barrier was a little too large to enter the gate to the lane and a few minutes were necessary to remove one of the supports temporarily.

The men in charge of the party repeatedly gave orders to make the whole proceeding as noiseless as possible. Once, a coolie was pounding with a hammer and received a curt order to pound more silently.

There was no evidence that electricity, gas, water had been cut off from the houses.

No Watching Crowd

The stealth of the attack had its reward for people sleeping in the immediate vicinity continued to sleep and there was no watching crowd despite the fact that the regions was obviously well populated. The terrace of houses that were blockaded are almost invisible from Ferry Road being behind the shops facing the street.

Earlier Blockade

Although the reason for this action on the part of the Shanghai Municipal Council could not be ascertained last night—due to the utmost air of secrecy which prevailed even as the last nail was being driven in—the creation of this little city within a city was very similar to the action taken in the case of recalcitrant Yu Yuen Road tax-payers last March. With this difference, however, that whereas last night's "besieged city" was entirely within Settlement limits, the barricaded terrace in March was actually in extra-Settlement territory, with entrances onto extra-Settlement roads maintained by the Municipal Council.

The recalcitrant tax-payers of the March affair included a number of Shanghai City Government officials and a Chinese lawyer, Mr. S. Y. Yeh, who threatened to sue the Council if the barricades were not removed. Taxes were owed by some of the defaulting ratepayers as far back as the last quarter of 1936.. The tenants of the houses concerned were duly warned by the Council, and when they remained obdurate the Council, after a further period of grace, struck quickly on the night of March 11.

The terraces concerned consisted of a vast compound of modern apartment buildings largely inhabited by Chinese; a total of 127 flats and several hundred people were shut off by the Council from the Settlement. Large bodies of police constables, including the Reserve Unit and their "Red Marias," stood by, in contrast to last night's bare handful of police officers. Inside the little "town," the Chinese Police were keeping order with the assistance of rifles with fixed bayonets.

Former Agreement

The barricades remained in place until the late afternoon of March 17, following which sewerage and water-drainage systems, which had been cut off in the meantime, were restored. An agreement with regard to the "lifting" of the siege was entered into between the Shanghai Municipal Council and the Shanghai City Government, the main point of the agreement being that the taxes were to be paid over to the City Government, that the two bodies should open negotiations regarding the payment of the tax in the future, and that in the event of the negotiations breaking down, the tax money should be handed over to the Council by the City Government.

S.
C.S.S. Sil
C. ½

《字林西报》，1937年8月5日，星期四

工部局路障
将房屋隔离
于渡轮路之外

工部局午夜
突然出击

极度保密

此举让人回想起
愚园路税务事件

昨晚午夜迅速出击，上海公共租界工部局的人员用装有铁丝网的木板封锁了渡轮路427弄的一排房屋。这支由工务局（P.W.D.）苦力组成的小分队从戈登路（Gordon Road）警察局悄悄出发，抵达弄堂并在二十分钟内快速高效地完成了任务。

工部局这一出乎意料的举动，与今年3月11日该机构在愚园路制造“紫禁城”、隔离一栋欠税房屋的行为几乎完全相同。

昨晚的整个行动明显试图保持极度机密。除了工部局人员、几名外籍警员、华捕以及约二十名工务局苦力外，现场唯一的旁观者是《字林西报》的代表。

与去年三月的封锁不同，昨晚的事件没有引起任何骚动或摩擦，部分原因或许是因为此次处理的房屋位于公共租界内，而非华界。

周密安排

显然事先已做了周密安排，因为弄堂两个入口的路障严丝合缝。这排房屋的每个入口都通向一条弄堂，两条弄堂相距约100码。完成一处工作后，小分队沿街道移动到另一个入口。在这里，由于计算失误，工作耽搁了几分钟。路障稍大，无法进入弄堂大门，因此需要几分钟时间暂时拆除其中一个支撑物。

带队人员反复命令整个行动尽可能保持无声。有一次，一名苦力用锤子敲击，接到了一道简短的命令，要求更安静地敲击。

没有证据表明房屋的电、气、水供应被切断。

无围观人群

偷袭的隐蔽性得到了回报，附近熟睡的人们继续安睡，尽管该地区人口显然稠密，但并无围观人群。被封锁的那排房屋从渡轮路上几乎看不见，因为它们位于临街店铺的后方。

此前的封锁

尽管由于甚至在最最后一颗钉子钉入时仍弥漫着极度保密的气氛，昨晚无法查明上海公共租界工部局采取此行动的原因——但这种在城中造城的举动与去年三月对付顽固的愚园路纳税人的行动非常相似。然而，区别在于，昨晚的“围城”完全位于租界范围内，而三月份被封锁的那排房屋实际上位于越界区域，其入口通往由工部局维护的越界道路。

三月事件中的顽固纳税人包括数名上海市政府官员和一位中国律师叶先生（Mr. S. Y. Yeh，音译），他威胁称若不拆除路障将起诉工部局。部分欠税纳税人的税款拖欠至1936年第四季度。工部局 duly 警告了相关房屋的租户，当他们仍然固执己见时，工部局在经过一段宽限期后，于3月11日晚迅速采取行动。

涉及的联排房屋由一个大型现代公寓建筑群组成，主要居住着中国人；工部局将总共127套公寓和数百人与租界隔离开来。大批警员，包括后备队及其“红玛丽亚”（Red Marias，音译，指特定制服或车辆）在一旁待命，这与昨晚寥寥无几的警员形成鲜明对比。在这个小“城镇”内部，华捕在配有刺刀的步枪协助下维持秩序。

先前协议

路障一直保留到3月17日下午晚些时候，随后恢复了在此期间被切断的污水和排水系统。上海公共租界工部局与上海市政府就“解除”包围达成了协议，协议的主要内容是税款应移交给市政府，双方应就未来的税款缴纳问题进行谈判，如果谈判破裂，市政府应将税款移交给工部局。

S.
C.S.S. Sil
C. ½

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Thursday, August 5, 1937.

Tax Barricades
Removed At Noon

Rate-Dodgers Regain
Freedom After 12
Hours "Prison"

The barricades at three compounds of Ferry Road, erected by the S.M.C. at midnight, were removed by workmen of the Public Works Department at 1.30 o'clock this afternoon, 13½ hours after erection to force payment by Chinese residents of the land tax.

Residents in three compounds located in lanes off Ferry Road and on Melchow Road were today receiving their food through wooden and barbed wire barricades erected by the Public Works Department at midnight, after the S.M.C. had decided that drastic steps were necessary to force the payment of land tax owners of unregistered land in the Settlement has thus been curtailed is not believed to exceed 300 and the barricades at two places are expected to be down some time late today when property owners meet the Council's demands.

Mr. Stirling Fessenden, secretary-general of the S.M.C., explained to a representative of this paper today that no question of municipal rates was involved in the present dispute, these having been paid regularly. The trouble centers around an old land registration law whereby land in the Settlement had to be registered with a foreign consul. Only land registered by a foreigner was taxed. Although most Chinese registered their land through some foreign subject, some never did this and even today their land is still under old Chinese deeds and

titles. These have not paid land tax.

Said Unfair

About nine months ago the Council decided that it was not fair that these land owners should enjoy all the amenities of municipal developments without paying taxes the same as other owners. A request was made for owners of unregistered land to pay the land tax. Some complied, others did not. Other measures having failed, the Council feels that those not paying should be prevented from using municipal roads. The total amount owned is not known.

Unlike the blockade in Yu Yuen Road on March 11, property affected today is in the Settlement. The blockade is also more effective, no possible means of exit being open to those within the barricades. Inhabitants are still receiving water, gas and electricity.

Factory Barricaded

At Lane 427, Ferry Road, about 40 members of the Soy Chong Brass and Iron Works were "imprisoned." Most of those inside were merely the apprentices as the regular workers lived outside the compound. Mr. William Kwok, who is in charge of the plant which employs about 70 persons, his family and the apprentices comprise the entire colony. The apprentices were hard at work this morning as usual, the clang of their hammers being plainly heard, but workers had an enforced holiday, being unable to enter. One foreign sergeant and one Chinese constable were on hand to see that the barricades were not broken.

Mr. Kwok claims that his firm had paid rates regularly and that the owner of the land, Mr. Sing Fook-kee, building contractor, was responsible for payment of land taxes. He also expected the barricades to be removed this afternoon. Only 27 Chinese bungalows and the factory are within the compound. Back taxes here are said to total only 54., according to Kwok.

Tongue-Lashing

In Lane 617 along the same road a representative of this paper found a Chinese woman giving a foreign police sergeant a tongue-lashing through a barred window of her house. She lived in a compound of about six new Chinese two-story stucco dwellings. Seven barricades were needed to keep residents in this area inside, but the results were effective, the only possible egress being over high walls.

The other place reported to be barricaded is at 300 Melchow Road where the Universal Industrial Corporation is located.

The S.M.C. denies that the present action is part of a campaign and claims that similar moves have been made during the past nine months. It merely considers it unfair that while some owners pay the land tax, others enjoy the same privileges free. Probably tax for the past nine months will only be demanded.

《上海晚邮报与水星报》，1937年8月5日，星期四。

中午拆除
税务路障

逃税者在12小时“监禁”后重获自由

工部局于午夜在渡船路（Ferry Road）三个里弄住宅区设置的路障，于今日下午1时30分由工务局工人拆除，此时距设置路障以迫使中国居民缴纳地税已过去13个半小时。

位于渡船路支弄及梅卓路（Melchow Road）的三个里弄住宅区的居民，今日通过工务局于午夜设置的木制及铁丝网路障接收食物。此前，工部局决定采取严厉措施，以迫使租界内未登记土地的所有者缴纳地税。据信，因此受到限制的土地所有者人数不超过300人，预计今日晚些时候，当业主满足工部局的要求后，两处地点的路障将被拆除。

工部局总董费森登（Stirling Fessenden）先生今日向本报代表解释称，目前的争端不涉及市政捐税问题，这些捐税一直定期缴纳。纠纷的核心在于一项古老的土地登记法规，根据该法规，租界内的土地必须向外国领事注册。只有由外国人注册的土地才需纳税。虽然大多数中国人通过某位外籍人士注册其土地，但有些人从未这样做，甚至直到今天，他们的土地仍持有旧式中国地契和产权证明。这些人尚未缴纳地税。

称不公平

大约九个月前，工部局决定，这些土地所有者在不与其他业主一样缴纳税款的情况下享受市政发展的所有便利设施是不公平的。当局要求未登记土地的业主缴纳地税。一些人照办了，另一些人则没有。在其他措施均告失败后，工部局认为应禁止那些不缴税的人使用市政道路。欠款总额尚不清楚。

与3月11日愚园路（Yu Yuen Road）的封锁不同，今日受影响的物业位于租界内。此次封锁也更为有效，路障内的人员没有任何可能的出口。居民仍可接收水、煤气和电力供应。

工厂被围

在渡船路427弄，约40名松昌铜铁厂（Soy Chong Brass and Iron Works）的成员被“囚禁”。里面的人大多是学徒，因为正式工人住在里弄外。郭威廉（William Kwok）先生负责这家雇佣约70人的工厂，他的家人和学徒构成了整个社区的全部人员。学徒们今早像往常一样努力工作，锤击声清晰可闻，但正式工人被迫休假，无法进入。一名外籍巡长和一名华捕在现场确保路障不被破坏。

郭先生声称，他的公司一直定期缴纳捐税，土地所有者、建筑承包商盛福记（Sing Fook-kee，音译）先生负责缴纳地税。他也预计路障将于今日下午拆除。据郭先生称，该里弄内仅有27栋中式平房和该工厂。这里的欠税总额据说仅为54元。

厉声斥责

在同一条路的617弄，本报记者发现一名中国妇女透过她家装有铁栏的窗户，对一名外籍巡长进行厉声斥责。她住在一个由大约六栋新建的两层中式灰泥住宅组成的里弄内。需要七道路障才能将该地区的居民困在里面，但效果显著，唯一的可能出口是翻越高墙。

据报道被设置路障的另一处地点是梅卓路300号，环球实业公司（Universal Industrial Corporation）所在地。

工部局否认目前的行动是一场运动的一部分，并声称在过去九个月中曾采取过类似的举措。工部局仅仅认为，当一些业主缴纳地税时，另一些人却免费享受同样的特权，这是不公平的。可能只会追缴过去九个月的税款。

Tax Plan For
Outside Roads
Told In Report

Settlement Would Get

51% Of Levies

The understanding reached between the City Government of Greater Shanghai and the Shanghai Municipal Council on the apportioning of rates and taxes in the extra-Settlement road areas as well as on the problem of police administration was revealed here yesterday in a Chinese press dispatch from Nanking.

According to this report, the tentative agreement, hitherto unrevealed, is said to have provided that the Council would receive 49 per cent of the total tax and rate receipts of the outside road areas, while the City Government will receive 51 per cent of the levies.

A special police bureau, according to the dispatch, would be organized with a Chinese as head of the organization. He would be assisted by a foreign assistant commissioner. The tentative agreement, recently initialed by Mr. O. K. Yui, Acting Mayor, and Mr. Stirling Fessenden, S.M.C. Secretary-General, is reported to have established he right of the Chinese to police the area.

The Japanese protest to the tentative agreement, it was stated, is not likely to affect this arrangement. Although the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Nanking had received no official information of the proposals made by Mr. N. Yoshioka, Japanese Consul, it was revealed that the points now at issue concern the telephone question and the geographical demarcation of the outside roads area.

The Japanese memorandum proposed that the service of the Shanghai Telephone Company should be extended to the outside road district without any royalty charges by the Chinese Telephone Administration. Also, the proposals suggested that areas lying 100 meters from the road should be included in the extra-Settlement road area.

THE CHINA PRESS, FRIDAY, MAY 7, 1937
Japanese Roads Plan
Referred To O. K. Yui
Council Hears Explanation Of Proposals But
Defers Action Until Later

After seven years of protracted negotiations, marked by repeated deadlocks, the extra-Settlement road issue, together with the pressing problem of obtaining a solution satisfactory to all interests, again confronted members of the Shanghai Municipal Council yesterday as they made a preliminary study of the latest Japanese proposals at their regular meeting yesterday afternoon.

No headway was made yesterday by the Council in adopting definite action regarding the memorandum on the outside road question recently presented to its Secretary-General, Mr. Stirling Fessenden, by Mr. N. Yoshioka, Acting Japanese Consul-General.

At the present time, the formal Japanese proposals are being studied by Mr. O. K. Yui, Acting Mayor of Greater Shanghai. Before his views are conveyed to the Council, the latter is not likely to act on the question.

Fessenden Explains

During the meeting yesterday afternoon, Mr. Fessenden made a brief explanation and report on the Japanese memorandum. The Councilmen were informed of the implications of the proposals, especially with regard to the negotiations which had been going on for the past seven years.

At the suggestion of Mr. Cornell S. Franklin, Council Chairman, discussion on the issue was postponed until a later date when the views of the City Government of Greater Shanghai are known.

As public interest continued to mount yesterday on the city's most controversial problem, much speculation was aroused over the contents and import of Mr. Yoshioka's proposals.

Apart from the fact that the Japanese memorandum deals with rates, tax, police, public utilities and other problems in the outside road areas, nothing is known regarding the specific suggestions of the plan. The Council, at the request of Mr. Yoshioka, has kept the proposals confidential.

In a conversation with Mr. Fessenden yesterday, a CHINA PRESS reporter was given to understand that the obstacles which blocked the solution of the extra-Settlement question in 1935 might again threaten to deadlock the present negotiations.

At that time, the modus vivendi worked out by Mr. Fessenden and Mr. Yui was rejected by Mr. Itaro Ishii, then Japanese Consul-General at Shanghai.

To allay Japanese objections, subsequent talks were conducted between Mr. Fessenden, Mr. Yui and Mr. Ishii, resulting in a satisfactory solution of practically all the major points at issue. A final solution of the outside road issue, however, was balked by two problems on which the Japanese were unwilling to accept any compromise.

The first problem at that time was the geographical demarcation of the outside road areas. Despite the fact that the City Government was willing to mark areas 100 meters from the outside roads as within the boundary of the extra-Settlement road, the Japanese refused to accept such a compromise choosing to stand pat on more drastic demands.

Phone Issue Disputed

The second point which ultimately deadlocked the negotiations in 1935 was on the telephone question. The Japanese insisted that in the outside road area, the residents be allowed to use the service of the Shanghai Telephone Company. This demand, the Chinese refused to accept, stating that the outside road area is in the Chinese territory and it therefore should be served by the Chinese Telephone Administration.

A compromise on this problem was later worked out. The City Government was willing to agree to the extension of the Shanghai Telephone Company service to the area if the subscribers would pay $60 royalty to the Chinese Telephone Administration. This was, however, considered again as unacceptable by the Japanese.

While much of the information on the extra-Settlement road negotiations during the past year were unrevealed to the public, THE CHINA PRESS was informed that the two points on telephone and geographical demarcation formed the chief obstacle which blocked a solution of the question in 1935.

Observers believe that the events leading to the 1935 deadlock will shed light on the present negotiations in view of the fact that the main points of Mr. Yoshioka's memorandum may center around the proposal made two years ago by his predecessor.

Reported Japanese proposal to turn the Outside Road areas in Hongkew into a semblance of a Japanese Concession has drawn the fire of Chinese residents in Hongkew.

At a meeting of the Executive Committee, of the Hongkew Residents Association held at noon yesterday, it was decided officially to bring the matter to the attention of the First Special District People's Association with the request the City Government of Greater Shanghai be urged to lodge a strong protest against the Japanese proposal.

《字林西报》，1937年5月7日，星期五
日本道路计划
转交俞鸿钧（O. K. Yui）
工部局听取提案说明但
推迟采取行动

经过七年旷日持久的谈判，其间屡陷僵局，界外道路问题以及寻求令各方利益均感满意的解决方案这一紧迫难题，昨日再次摆在上海公共租界工部局董事面前。在昨日下午的例行会议上，董事们对日本方面的最新提案进行了初步研究。

工部局昨日在就日本代理总领事吉冈（N. Yoshioka）先生近期提交给工部局总秘书费信惇（Stirling Fessenden）先生的关于界外道路问题的备忘录采取明确行动方面，未取得任何进展。

目前，大上海代市长俞鸿钧（O. K. Yui）先生正在研究日本的正式提案。在其意见传达至工部局之前，工部局不太可能就此问题采取行动。

费信惇作出解释

在昨日下午的会议上，费信惇先生就日本备忘录作了简要说明和报告。各位董事获悉了该提案的含义，特别是涉及过去七年一直进行的谈判的相关情况。

根据工部局董事会主席富兰克林（Cornell S. Franklin）先生的建议，关于此问题的讨论被推迟至日后，待大上海市政府的意见明朗后再行进行。

随着公众昨日对这一本市最具争议问题的兴趣持续高涨，吉冈先生提案的内容和意图引发了诸多猜测。

除了得知日本备忘录涉及界外道路区域的费率、税收、警务、公用事业及其他问题外，该计划的具体建议内容无人知晓。应吉冈先生的要求，工部局对提案内容予以保密。

一位《字林西报》记者昨日在与费信惇先生交谈时了解到，1935年阻碍解决界外道路问题的障碍可能再次威胁到当前的谈判，使其陷入僵局。

当时，由费信惇先生和俞鸿钧先生制定的临时办法遭到了时任日本驻上海总领事石射猪太郎（Itaro Ishii）先生的拒绝。

为了消除日方的反对意见，费信惇先生、俞鸿钧先生和石射先生随后进行了会谈，结果实际上所有主要争议点都达成了令人满意的解决方案。然而，界外道路问题的最终解决因两个日方不愿接受任何妥协的问题而受阻。

当时的第一个问题是界外道路区域的地理划界。尽管市政府愿意将界外道路两侧100米内的区域划为界外道路范围，但日方拒绝接受这种妥协，坚持更为苛刻的要求。

电话问题引发争议

最终导致1935年谈判僵局的第二个点是电话问题。日方坚持要求在界外道路区域内，居民可以使用上海电话公司的服务。中方拒绝接受这一要求，称界外道路区域属于中国领土，因此应由中华电话局提供服务。

后来就此问题达成了一项妥协方案。市政府同意将上海电话公司的服务延伸至该区域，前提是用户需向中华电话局支付60美元的特许权使用费。然而，日方再次认为这是不可接受的。

虽然过去一年中关于界外道路谈判的大部分信息未向公众披露，但《字林西报》获悉，电话和地理划界这两点是阻碍1935年问题解决的主要障碍。

观察家认为，鉴于吉冈先生备忘录的要点可能围绕其前任两年前提出的提案展开，导致1935年僵局的事件将为目前的谈判提供启示。

据报道，日本提议将虹口界的界外道路区域变成类似日本租界的形态，这引起了虹口中国居民的强烈反对。

在昨日中午举行的虹口居民协会执行委员会会议上，正式决定将此事项提请注意第一特区市民联合会，并请求敦促大上海市政府对日本提案提出强烈抗议。

The Japanese proposals on the latest tentative plan to settle this question, and the Chinese views on these proposals, will be presented to the Councillors by Mr. Stirling Fessenden, secretary-general of the S.M.C., and a discussion is on the agenda.

Mr. N. Yoshioka, acting Japanese consul-general, has handed Mr. Fessenden the Japanese plans to revise the draft agreement, but these proposals have been kept secret from the public on request of the Japanese official. Mr. Fessenden will acquaint the Council with the nature of these proposals, as well as report on the Chinese views as expressed by Mr. O. K. Yui, acting mayor of the Municipality, with whom Mr. Fessenden conferred yesterday.

Thorny Problem

These proposals deal with the outside road tax and rate problems, administration, police and public utility issues.

The outside roads question has been a thorn in the side of Shanghai officials for the past seven years, ever since negotiations were started to establish their status and jurisdiction. Every time an agreement has appeared imminent other suggestions have been made blocking the final settlement, these blockades usually having been set up by the Japanese. The Japanese object strenuously to Chinese control of the areas, particularly in the northern road extensions, as Japanese interests there are large and many nationals live in that district.

Deny "Concession" Sought

The Japanese deny, however, that they are demanding a "concession" for themselves in the northern district, as rumored among the Chinese. They state that the outside roads constitute "special areas" and should be administered by a joint commission with specially appointed officers.

Another problem slated to be brought to the attention of the Council this afternoon is the Industrial Section report on the municipal problem in Shanghai. This report was made in full several weeks ago and now proposals for implementing the suggestions to alleviate the situation are to be brought up for approval.

棘手问题

这些提案涉及界外道路的税收和费率问题、行政管理、警务和公用事业问题。

自开始谈判以确定界外道路的地位和管辖权以来，界外道路问题在过去七年中一直是上海官员的心头之患。每当协议看似即将达成时，总会有其他建议提出，阻碍最终解决，这些阻碍通常由日方设置。日方强烈反对中方控制这些区域，特别是在北部道路延伸段，因为日方在那里的利益巨大，且有许多日本国民居住在该区。

否认寻求“租界”

然而，日方否认如中方传闻的那样，他们是在为自己在北区要求一个“租界”。他们声称，界外道路构成“特殊区域”，应由一个设有特别任命官员的联合委员会进行管理。

今天下午提请工部局注意的另一个问题是工业科关于上海市政问题的报告。该报告已在数周前完整提交，现在实施缓解局势建议的提案将提请批准。

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, THURSDAY, MAY 6, 1937

Concession Is

Special Area Is Sought

On Outside Roads

POLICING AGREEMENT

Emphatic denials were given last night in reliable Japanese circles to the report current in a section of the local Chinese press to the effect that the Japanese were demanding that, as a prerequisite to a settlement of the Outside Roads controversy, a "concession" be set aside for the Japanese in the northern district.

It was admitted, however, that the Japanese regarded the Outside Roads districts as "special areas" and that they should be administered as such by a joint commission with specially appointed officers.

A section of the vernacular press last night reported that one of the proposals submitted to the Shanghai Municipal Council and the Shanghai City Government regarding the terms of settlement of the controversy regarding the Outside Roads was that a large area in the Northern (Hongkew) District should be regarded as a "concession" for the Japanese. This was vigorously denied in reliable Japanese quarters.

As was pointed out previously, the Japanese consider that any agreement on the Outside Roads between the S.M.C. and the City Government should not be confined to the fiscal side alone. If an agreement is to be reached it must be on the whole issue, the Japanese contend. This embraces not only the collection of rates and taxes, but the question of policing, health, fire protection and other matters relevant to the welfare of residents in these areas.

Same Old Problem

When the same position arose several years ago the proposal was made that the districts involved, and which were considered outside S.M.C. jurisdiction, should come under the supervision of joint Chinese and foreign control. It was then suggested that a foreign police officer should be approved by the Chinese and foreign authorities and that Chinese officers should also be appointed to act with him in supervising the disputed areas.

No satisfactory conclusion was reached on this matter and the modus vivendi which was then drawn up lapsed until recently revived by discussions between Mr. O. K. Yui and Mr. Stirling Fessenden. Recently a tentative agreement was reached between these two representatives, but when submitted to members of the Council for consideration, a full Council discussion on the subject was postponed in deference to the wishes of the Japanese members of the S.M.C.

In the meantime new proposals were submitted to the Council by Japanese representatives, these in turn being submitted to the Consular Body and these will to-day be considered by the Council.

The exact nature of the proposals has not been disclosed, but it is known that they involve a much wider aspect of the whole problem than the mere collection of taxes on the Outside Roads.

昨晚，可靠的日本方面人士断然否认了本地中文报刊部分版面流传的报道。该报道称，日本人要求将北区划出一块“租界”，作为解决越界筑路争议的先决条件。

然而，日方承认，他们将越界筑路地区视为“特别区”，并认为应由一个拥有特别任命官员的联合委员会对此类地区进行管理。

昨晚，部分中文报刊报道，在提交给上海公共租界工部局和上海市政府的关于解决越界筑路争议条款的提案中，有一项建议是将北区（虹口）的大片区域视为日本的“租界”。这一说法遭到了可靠的日本方面的强烈否认。

正如先前指出的那样，日本人认为，工部局与市政府之间关于越界筑路的任何协议都不应仅局限于财政方面。日方主张，如果要达成协议，必须涵盖整个问题。这不仅包括捐税征收，还包括警务、卫生、消防以及其他与该地区居民福利有关的事项。

老问题重现

几年前出现同样情况时，曾有人提议，将那些被认为不在工部局管辖范围内的涉及地区，置于中外联合监管之下。当时建议，由中外当局批准一名外籍警官，并任命华籍警官与其共同监督争议地区。

此事未达成令人满意的结论，当时拟定的临时安排随后失效，直到最近经由余井塘先生与费信惇先生的讨论才得以重启。近期，这两位代表达成了初步协议，但在提交给工部局董事审议时，出于对工部局日籍董事意愿的尊重，董事会关于此议题的全面讨论被推迟。

与此同时，日本代表向工部局提交了新提案，这些提案又转交给了领事团，工部局将于今日对这些提案进行审议。

提案的确切性质尚未披露，但据悉，这些提案涉及整个问题的更广泛层面，而不仅仅是越界筑路的税收征收。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, FRIDAY, APRIL 23, 1937

Outside Roads
Taxation Issue
Troubles S.M.C.

Fessenden-Yui Agreement
Under Japanese Fire

A DELICATE SITUATION

Threat of “Ideal Special
District”

The new Shanghai Municipal Council has begun work in earnest. At its first ordinary meeting on Wednesday the consideration of the tentative agreement on Outside Road taxation reported to have been reached by discussion between Mr. O. K. Yui, the Acting Mayor of the City Government, and Mr. Stirling Fessenden, Secretary-General of the Council was postponed to permit Japanese Members to study its conditions. This was followed yesterday by an emergency meeting, at which it is understood the Council had the full position in regard to the Yui-Fessenden talks explained to it by Mr. Fessenden himself. The tenour of the exposition was not officially disclosed, just as no formal statement was forthcoming after the meeting on Wednesday, but it is clear, from observations made to a representative of the “North-China Daily News” by a resident well in touch with Chinese opinion, that a delicate situation has arisen. Referring directly to this journal’s comment yesterday and, particularly to its warning

“The danger of delay has been consistently preferred to the risk of making an agreement which at the time seemed to be insufficiently guarded at all points. The result—and careful study of the course of events right up to the Tifeng Road affair confirms this view—has been that ground held by the Council at one time has been made untenable subsequently”

the informant declared that it accurately summed up the position from the Chinese point of view.

It is gathered that, as the Chinese municipal authorities virtually came to the Council’s rescue in the Tifeng Road settlement, they are not disposed to accept any proposals less favourable than implied therein. This attitude is believed to have found expression in the provisional agreement to which Mr. Fessenden is said to have put his initials, he being, as the result of seven years’ experience, thoroughly aware of the impressions created by frequent approaches to solution, followed almost immediately by as frequent resettlements, of which the latest example is thought to have been given by the new Council’s postponement on Wednesday.

The Japanese View

The Chinese view is not the only factor in this problem. Japanese opinion is forcibly against any limited agreement—that is an agreement which deals merely with the collection of taxation, leaving the administrative issues such as policing and sanitation to be dealt with later. It is possible therefore, that the Council will be between two fires: Chinese determination to stand on the offer made by Mr. O. K. Yui; with the covert hint that if it be not accepted the next one will be less favourable; Japanese insistence on the treatment of the Outside Roads problem as a whole, backed up with the intimation that the alternative may be the carving out of a Japanese “special area” for the satisfaction of Japanese notions of security.

It is, however, pointed out that the Council, unwittingly or otherwise, has already gone far to establish the principle that the City Government should be responsible for collecting taxes on the Outside Roads and for passing the revenue on to the Council after deduction of an agreed percentage which is understood to be the main feature of the Yui-Fessenden draft agreement. Leaving out of account the Tifeng Road collections by which the principle was recognized it is evident that the Council has acquiesced in the City Government’s assertion of its authority in, for example, the negotiations with labour. The now settled tram strike was apparently the subject of no effort on the Council’s part. The City Government took the initiative in dealing with the strikers, as it had done on other recent occasions of labour unrest. Yet the trams operating in the Settlement do so under a Council franchise.

Utility Companies’ Action

Similarly the separate negotiations, successfully conducted by the Telephone Company and the Shanghai Power Company with the City Government, although those concerns are Utility Companies with Council franchises, are looked upon as definitely impairing the Council’s authority on the Outside Roads, or, rather, taking from the Council the power to maintain more than the position taken up by Mr. Fessenden in the discussions with Mr. Yui.

The seriousness of the outlook lies in the fact that the Council may be faced by the choice between a reversion to the rigid attitude which appears to be favoured by the Japanese, and a prompt endorsement of the Fessenden-Yui pact, subject to the reservation that it leaves entirely open the administrative issues to which the Japanese attach special importance. It is doubtful whether the Japanese at the present would be placated by such reservation. Altogether the new Council seems likely to receive an early baptism of political fire.

Japanese Press Comment

Taking issue with critics of the Japanese official attitude towards the conclusion of an accord between the Shanghai Municipal Council and the Municipality of Greater Shanghai for the collection of taxes in extra-Settlement areas, the local Japanese press discussed the issue in lengthy editorials yesterday.

The gist of the contentions advanced by both the Shanghai “Nippo” and the Shanghai “Mainichi” was that a solution of the whole extension roads question should be sought at this time, instead of limiting the agreement to the tax issue alone.

《字林西报》，1937年4月23日，星期五

越界筑路
税收问题
工部局陷入困境

费森登-俞鸿钧协议
遭日本方面抨击

局势微妙

“理想特别区”之威胁

新一届上海公共租界工部局董事会已认真开始工作。在周三举行的第一次常会上，关于越界筑路税收的暂定协议（据报由上海特别市政府代理市长俞鸿钧先生与工部局总董费森登先生经讨论达成）的审议被推迟，以便让日籍董事研究其条款。随后于昨日召开了一次紧急会议，据悉，费森登先生亲自向董事会全面解释了他在与俞鸿钧会谈中的立场。此次说明的要旨并未正式披露，正如周三会议后未发表正式声明一样；但据一位熟悉中国舆论的人士向《字林西报》记者表示，显然出现了一种微妙的局面。该人士直接提及本报昨日的评论，特别是其中的警告：

“人们一贯认为，延误的危险小于达成一项在当时看来各方面保障均不足的协议的风险。其结果——且对直至提篮桥路事件为止的事态发展进程的仔细研究证实了这一观点——是，董事会一度占据的立场随后变得站不住脚。”

该消息人士宣称，这准确地概括了从中方角度看待的局势。

据了解，由于中国市政当局在提篮桥路事件的解决中实际上救助了工部局，他们不愿接受任何不如该事件中所隐含条件有利的提议。据信，这种态度已体现在费森登先生据说已草签的临时协议中；凭借七年的经验，他充分意识到频繁寻求解决方案、随即又频繁重新安排所造成的印象，而新董事会周三的推迟被视为最新的例证。

日本方面的观点

在此问题中，中方观点并非唯一因素。日本舆论强烈反对任何有限度的协议——即仅处理税收征收，而将警务和卫生等行政问题留待日后处理的协议。因此，工部局可能处于两面夹击之中：中方坚持要求以俞鸿钧先生提出的报价为基础，并暗中暗示若不被接受，下一次的条件将更加不利；日方则坚持将越界筑路问题作为一个整体来处理，并暗示替代方案可能是划出一个日本的“特别区域”，以满足日本人的安全观念。

然而，有人指出，无论有意还是无意，工部局已在很大程度上确立了这样一个原则，即市政府应负责征收越界筑路地区的税款，并在扣除商定百分比后将收入转交工部局，这被认为是俞鸿钧-费森登协议草案的主要特征。撇开据以承认该原则的提篮桥路税收征收不谈，显然工部局已默许市政府行使其权威，例如在与劳工的谈判中。目前已平息的电车罢工显然未耗费工部局任何努力。市政府主动处理罢工者，正如它在近期其他劳工动荡事件中所做的那样。然而，在租界内运营的电车是依据工部局的特许权经营的。

公用事业公司的行动

同样，电话公司和上海电力公司与市政府分别进行的成功谈判，尽管这些公司是拥有工部局特许权的公用事业公司，也被视为明确损害了工部局在越界筑路地区的权威，或者说，剥夺了工部局维持比费森登先生在与俞鸿钧先生讨论中所持立场更有利地位的能力。

前景的严峻性在于，工部局可能面临两种选择：一是回归到似乎受日本方面青睐的强硬态度，二是迅速认可费森登-俞鸿钧协定，但保留意见是，该协定将日本人特别重视的行政问题完全搁置。目前日本人是否会因这种保留意见而感到平息，尚存疑问。总之，新董事会似乎很可能很快经历一场政治战火的洗礼。

日本报刊评论

针对批评日本官方对上海公共租界工部局与大上海市政府就租界外地区税收征收达成协议的态度，当地日本报纸昨日发表长篇社论讨论此问题。

上海《日日新闻》和上海《每日新闻》所提出论点的主旨是，此时应寻求解决整个越界筑路问题，而不是将协议仅限于税收问题。

越界筑路
税收协定
避免冲突

董事会推迟讨论关键议题至下次会议

仅处理常规事务

与此同时，费森登将寻求与日本人妥协

为了避免来自两名日籍董事的正面攻击，新一届上海公共租界工部局董事会在昨日下午的第一次业务会议上，推迟了对有争议的租界外道路税收问题的讨论。

该问题围绕市政府与工部局之间最近草签的关于境外税收征收的协议展开，已被推迟至5月5日的下一次董事会会议。

在此期间，预计工部局将通过其总董费森登先生，消除当地日本社区提出的反对意见，后者以未能考虑日本人利益为由，强烈反对这项临时税收协定。

日本代理总领事吉冈 N. 先生曾于周一拜访费森登先生，递交其政府的正式抗议，预计他将根据其在沪国民的观点提出一项妥协方案。

如果日本方面的提议被市政府和工部局双方认为可以接受，那么在再次提交董事会讨论之前，可能会对现行协定进行一些修改。

处理常规事务

原计划对临时协定采取行动的董事会会议，仅处理了议程上的一些常规任务。会议历时不到10分钟即休会。

与此同时，工部局尚未公布的临时协定内容，昨日在中外社区引发了更多猜测。该协定的要点近日由《大美晚报》独家披露，昨日得到非官方但极具权威的消息来源确认为属实。

支付公用事业费用

根据该协定，原则上承认市政府有权在越界筑路地区征收税款和捐率。市政府需将部分征收款项支付给工部局，作为对居民享受的公用事业和其他利益的补偿。

除上述几点外，昨日还获悉，将在越界筑路地区设立一个税务办公室，目的是征收税款。该机构将由市政府设立，其部分工作人员将由工部局提名。

Japanese
Protest

Rate Collection Move On

Objected To

IS TERMED “EXTREMELY

TOKYO, April 20.—The tentative agreement on the collection of taxes on extra-Settlement roads, reached recently between the Shanghai Municipal Council and the Municipality of Greater Shanghai, is meeting with opposition from Japan.

The Foreign Office here is learnt to-day to have instructed the Acting Consul-General in Shanghai, Mr. N. Yoshioka, to protest to the parties to the agreement against “the Council’s transfer of taxation rights in the extension areas to the Municipality of Greater Shanghai without the Japanese Government’s previous knowledge.”

The move is termed as “extremely unfriendly.”

The agreement in question, initialled on April 13 by Mr. S. Fessenden, Secretary-General of the Municipal Council, and Mr. O. K. Yui, Acting Mayor of the Municipality of Greater Shanghai, is reported to provide for the S.M.C.’s recognition, in principle, of the right of the City Government to collect taxes and rates in extra-Settlement roads.

It is also reported to stipulate that the Council is to act as proxy of the City Government in collecting taxes, and that a portion of the levies thus collected is to be paid to the S.M.C. by the City Government as compensation for public utilities and other benefits enjoyed by the residents in the outside areas.—Reuter.

据悉，日本外务省今日指示驻上海代理总领事吉冈 N. 先生，向协议各方抗议“工部局在未事先知会日本政府的情况下，将扩展区域的征税权移交给大上海市政府”。

此举被称为“极不友好”。

据悉，该协议由工部局总董费森登先生和大上海市政府代理市长俞鸿钧先生于4月13日草签，规定工部局原则上承认市政府在租界外道路征收税款和捐率的权利。

另据报道，协议规定工部局将作为市政府的代理人征收税款，市政府将把征收的部分款项支付给工部局，作为对境外地区居民享受的公用事业和其他利益的补偿。——路透社

THE CHINA PRESS, WEDNESDAY, APRIL 21, 1937
21324
JAPANESE OBSTRUCTION

THE extra-Settlement roads question which bids fair to be settled once for all is now again made the subject of unwarranted opposition from the Japanese. It is reported that Mr. N. Yoshioka, Japanese Consul, has made a personal call on Mr. Stirling Fessenden, Secretary-General of the Shanghai Municipal Council, and has reiterated the Japanese objection to the tentative agreement between the Council and the City Government of Greater Shanghai.

The chief point of dispute in the agreement under discussion is the collection of the municipal rate. The Chinese authorities have maintained that the Council has no right to tax the Chinese residents domiciled on the extra-Settlement roads, and the Council but recently saw fit to barricade one of the lanes on Yu Yuen Road as a test case. In consequence a compromise arrangement was made by which the Council is to act as the proxy of the City Government in the collection of the rate and to pay into the Chinese municipal coffer a percentage of the rate so collected.

The agreement is expected to iron out the most serious differences arising from the extra-Settlement roads, and no foreign nationals other than the Japanese have ventured to dispute the authority of the Council in entering into this agreement with the Chinese authorities.

The objection of the Japanese is not new. It was raised in 1932 and in 1934 and is raised once again. Exactly what the Japanese want is not known, nor have the Japanese been candid enough to tell the public what they want.

From a recent issue of The Shanghai Mainichi one gathers a faint impression of the Japanese wishes. As it says:

The local Japanese community . . . has continuously sought to bring about an amicable settlement of the (outside road) problem, in the desire of creating an ideal residential zone. On one hand, the Chinese have been engaged in the talk of the theory of sovereignty, and the S.M.C. has been hoping for a favorable turn in the situation, paying no attention to the needs of the residents. What is needed is a compromise agreement, which would consider the interests of the Japanese residents. . . . Why did the Council, aware of the possibility of a compromise agreement, make such a concession to the Chinese authorities?

The so-called “interests of the Japanese residents” are indefinable. Surely they cannot be different from those of any other national group in the Settlement; surely, the Japanese cannot object to the payment of the municipal rate in the same manner as all other residents. If they do not so object, then what interests could be possibly sacrificed by the Council in concluding the agreement in question with the City Government?

It is common knowledge, of course, that many Japanese residents have failed to pay rentals for houses they occupy in the Northern district under one legal pretext or another, and it is thus logical to presume that they would hardly be agreeable to the payment of the municipal rate. Yet what individual Japanese may choose to do is vitally different from what the Japanese Consul may officially say. Since Mr. Yoshioka has officially reiterated the Japanese objection to the agreement concerned, will he be so good as to enlighten the community on the legal basis on which the objection may be justified?

From The Mainichi one also reads of its reference to “the theory of sovereignty” which the Chinese have been “talking” about. This Japanese journal should be given to understand that the sovereignty of China is not a theory but a fact officially recognized by the Japanese Government. If it continues to be imprudent in its remarks, the Japanese Consul may perhaps of his own accord take disciplinary action to maintain the spirit of international comity just as the Chinese authorities did in upholding the dignity of the Japanese Throne against a Chinese journal.

At any rate the agreement, with or without the Japanese consent, should be signed and made binding on the Council and the Chinese City Government. Both parties thereto have full authority to act in the best interests of the community, and if the Japanese should refuse to pay the municipal rate, we believe the Council will not hesitate to take the same action against them as it did against the Chinese residents on Yu Yuen Road. The prestige of the Council is at stake, and nothing should be permitted to jeopardise it in any manner.

《字林西报》，1937年4月21日，星期三
21324
日本的阻挠

界外道路问题本有望一劳永逸地得到解决，如今却再次成为日本无理反对的对象。据悉，日本领事吉冈（N. Yoshioka，音译）先生已亲自拜访上海工部局总董费信惇（Stirling Fessenden）先生，并重申日方对工部局与大上海市政府之间达成的临时协议的反对意见。

正在讨论的协议中的主要争议点在于市政捐的征收。中方当局坚持认为，工部局无权向居住在界外道路的中国居民征税，而工部局最近决定在愚园路封锁一条弄堂作为测试案例。因此，双方达成了一项妥协安排，即由工部局作为市政府的代理征收市政捐，并将所收捐款的一定比例缴入中国市政库。

预计该协议将消除因界外道路问题而产生的最严重分歧，除日本人外，没有其他外籍人士敢于质疑工部局与中国当局签订此协议的权力。

日本的反对并非新鲜事。这一问题曾在1932年和1934年提出，如今再次被提起。日本究竟想要什么并不为人所知，日本人也未坦诚地向公众说明他们的诉求。

从最近一期《上海每日新闻》（The Shanghai Mainichi）中，人们可以隐约了解到日本的愿望。该报称：

当地日本侨民……一直寻求友好解决（界外道路）问题，以期创造一个理想的居住区。一方面，中国人一直在谈论主权理论，而上海工部局则希望局势出现有利转折，忽视了居民的需求。现在需要的是一项考虑到日本居民利益的妥协协议……既然工部局明知有可能达成妥协协议，为何还要对中国当局做出如此让步？

所谓“日本居民的利益”是无法定义的。当然，这些利益不可能与其他任何国籍的租界居民不同；当然，日本人不能像其他所有居民一样反对以相同方式缴纳市政捐。如果他们不反对此点，那么工部局在与市政府签订有关协议时，可能牺牲了什么利益呢？

众所周知，许多日本居民以各种法律借口为托辞，未能支付他们在北区所居住房屋的租金，因此合乎逻辑地推测，他们很难同意缴纳市政捐。然而，个别日本人的行为与日本领事的官方表态有着本质区别。既然吉冈先生已正式重申日方对相关协议的反对，他能否好心地向公众阐明这种反对意见得以成立的法律依据？

从《每日新闻》中还可以读到其提及中国人一直在“谈论”的“主权理论”。这家日本报刊应该明白，中国的主权不是一个理论，而是一个日本政府官方承认的事实。如果该报继续发表轻率的言论，日本领事或许会主动采取纪律行动，以维护国际礼让的精神，正如中国当局为维护日本天皇尊严而对一家中文报刊采取行动那样。

无论如何，无论日本是否同意，该协议都应签署并对工部局和中国市政府具有约束力。协议双方拥有充分的权力，可为社区的最佳利益行事，如果日本拒绝缴纳市政捐，我们相信工部局将毫不犹豫地对他们采取与对愚园路中国居民相同的行动。工部局的威望岌岌可危，不应允许以任何方式危及其威望。

THE CHINA PRESS. WEDNESDAY, APRIL 21, 1937 21336
Japanese Ire Stirred
By Extra Roads Tax
Plan; Protest Ordered

Tokyo Regards Accord
As "Extremely
Unfriendly"

FIREWORKS SEEN
AT COUNCIL MEET.

Japanese S. M. C. Mem-
bers Expected To
Voice Opposition

TOKYO, Apr. 20.—(Reuters).—
The tentative agreement on the
collection of taxes on extra-Settle-
ment roads, reached recently be-
tween the Shanghai Municipal
Council and the Municipality of
Greater Shanghai, is meeting with
opposition from Japan.

The Foreign Office here is learn-
ed today to have instructed the
Acting Consul-General in Shang-
hai, Mr. N. Yoshioka, to protest
to the parties to the agreement
against "the Council's transfer of
taxation rights in the extension
areas to the Municipality of
Greater Shanghai without the
Japanese Government's previous
knowledge."

The move is termed as "extreme-
ly unfriendly."

The agreement in question, ini-
tialled on April 13 by Mr. S. Fes-
senden, Secretary-General of the
Municipal Council, and Mr. O. K.
Yui, Acting Mayor of the Munici-
pality of Greater Shanghai, is re-
ported to provide for the S.M.C.'s
recognition, in principle, of the
right of the City Government to
collect taxes and rates in extra-
Settlement roads.

It is also reported to stipulate
that the Council is to act as proxy
of the City Government in collect-
ing taxes, and that a portion of
the levies thus collected is to be
paid to the S.M.C. by the City Gov-
ernment as compensation for pub-
lic utilities and other benefits en-
joyed by the residents in the out-
side areas.

Heated Council
Meeting Foreseen

A verbal bombardment against
the tentative agreement on extra-
Settlement road tax collection is
expected to be made by two
Japanese members of the Shanghai
Municipal Council this afternoon
when the preliminary road pact
comes up for discussion at the
Council meeting at 4.30 o'clock.

Although originally scheduled to
study the tentative pact and pos-
sibly to give its approval to the
contents, the meeting this after-
noon is now believed unlikely to
act on the agreement as a result
of the strenuous objection raised
by members of the Japanese com-
munity.

The stand of the local Japanese
was outlined to the Council Mon-
day when Mr. N. Yoshioka, acting
Japanese Consul-General, called
on Mr. Stirling Fessenden, S.M.C.
Secretary-General, to point out
that the provisions of the pact, as
it now stands, are not acceptable
to the Japanese.

See Little Hope

Contacted by THE CHINA PRESS
yesterday high officials of the
Council admitted that they see
little hope of an early solution
of the outside road question if the
Japanese refuse to change their
present attitude.

It was revealed that a so-called
compromise plan is now being
worked out by the Japanese. Mr.
Yoshioka is reported to be sche-
duled to present such a plan to
the Council in the near future.

Although the exact provisions of
the tentative pact are unknown, it
was stated that in the agreement
the S.M.C. recognizes, in principle
the right of the City Government
to collect taxes in the outside road
areas. It also stipulated that the
Council is to act by proxy for the
City Government in collecting the
levies. A portion of the taxes and
rates is to be paid to the Council
by the City Government as com-
pensation for public utilities and
other benefits enjoyed by the re-
sidents.

While the agreement is viewed as
a forerunner for a more compre-
hensive pact on the entire outside
road question, the fiscal arrange-
ment worked out is in itself urgent
and necessary from the point of
view of S.M.C. finances. It was re-
vealed that a large number of
residents, Japanese included, are
dodging tax payment to both the
Council and the City Government
as a result of the present status.

Unless a fiscal modus vivendi is
worked out, the Council will con-
tinue to lose a large amount of tax
money.

Use Similar Tactics

Observers recalled yesterday that
the stand now being taken by the
Japanese is similar to the one they
took last year in blocking the ten-
tative agreement on factory inspec-
tion.

At that time, when the factory
pact came up for the Council's
approval, the two Japanese mem-
bers cast the only dissenting votes.
Later when the pact was passed
on to the Consular Body, the ob-
jection of the Japanese Consul-
General finally succeeded in bring-
ing about a veto which resulted in
the foreign consuls' action in
throwing out the pact as unaccep-
table.

Five years ago, the Japanese ob-
jection resulted in the "shelving"
of the outside road negotiations
which up until that time had been
nearing a speedy solution. Later, in
1934, when the outside road ques-
tion again came up, the Japanese
Consul-General for the second
time blocked its final solution by
his stand.

《字林西报》，1937年4月21日，星期三 21336
界外道路征税计划激起日本怒火；下令抗议

东京视该协定为“极不友好”

工部局会议上预计将出现激烈场面。

预计上海工部局日本籍董事将表示反对

东京，4月20日——（路透社）。——上海工部局与大上海市政府近期就界外道路征税问题达成的临时协议，正遭到日本的反对。

据悉，日本外务省今日已指示驻上海代理总领事吉冈（N. Yoshioka，音译）先生，向协议各方提出抗议，反对“工部局在未事先知会日本政府的情况下，将扩展区域的征税权移交给大上海市政府”。

此举被称为“极不友好”。

据悉，该协议由工部局总秘书费森登（S. Fessenden，音译）先生和大上海市政府代理市长俞鸿钧（O. K. Yui，音译）先生于4月13日草签，规定工部局在原则上承认市政府在界外道路区域征收税捐的权利。

据称，协议还规定工部局将作为市政府的代理征收税捐，市政府将从所征税款中拨出一部分支付给工部局，作为对界外区域居民享受的公共设施及其他利益的补偿。

预计工部局会议气氛热烈

今天下午4时30分举行的工部局会议上，当初步道路协定提交讨论时，预计上海工部局的两名日本籍董事将对关于界外道路征税的临时协议发起口头抨击。

虽然原计划是研究该临时协定并可能批准其内容，但由于日本侨民成员提出的强烈反对，相信今天下午的会议不太可能就协议采取行动。

周一，代理日本总领事吉冈（N. Yoshioka，音译）先生拜访了工部局总秘书费信惇（Stirling Fessenden）先生，向工部局阐述了当地日本人的立场，指出就目前而言，该协定的条款是日本人所不能接受的。

希望渺茫

《字林西报》昨日联系工部局高级官员时，他们承认，如果日本人不改变目前的态度，他们看不到早日解决界外道路问题的希望。

据悉，日本人目前正在制定一项所谓的妥协方案。据报道，吉冈先生计划在不久的将来向工部局提交该方案。

虽然临时协定的确切条款尚不为人知，但据说在该协议中，工部局在原则上承认市政府在界外道路区域征税的权利。协议还规定，工部局将代理市政府征收税款。市政府将把部分税捐支付给工部局，作为对居民享受的公共设施及其他利益的补偿。

虽然该协议被视为就整个界外道路问题达成更全面协定的前奏，但从工部局财政的角度来看，所制定的财政安排本身是紧迫且必要的。据悉，由于目前的状况，大量居民（包括日本人）都在逃避向工部局和市政府缴纳税款。

除非制定出一种财政上的临时相处之道，否则工部局将继续损失大量税款。

使用类似策略

观察家们昨日回顾说，日本目前采取的立场与去年阻碍工厂检查临时协定时的立场相似。

当时，当工厂协定提交工部局批准时，两名日本籍董事投下了唯一的反对票。后来，当该协定转交领事团时，日本总领事的反对最终成功导致否决，致使外国领事们以不可接受为由驳回了该协定。

五年前，日本的反对导致界外道路谈判被“搁置”，而直到那时，谈判已接近迅速解决。后来，在1934年，当界外道路问题再次出现时，日本总领事以其立场第二次阻碍了其最终解决。

THE CHINA PRESS, TUESDAY, APRIL 20, 1937

Notice Given
Of Japanese
Objection On
Roads Pact

Consul Yoshioka Calls
At Council To State
Non-Acceptance

RECENT ACCORD
GIVEN SET-BACK

Inclusive Settlement Of
Extra Roads Issue
Now Prejudiced

Objection on the part of the local Japanese, similar in nature to the one they raised in 1932 and 1934, may again prevent an early solution of the extra-Settlement road question.

This was indicated yesterday when Mr. N. Yoshioka, Japanese Consul, called on Mr. Stirling Fessenden, Secretary General of the Shanghai Municipal Council, to point out formally that the tentative agreement on outside roads tax collections, reached between the City Government of Greater Shanghai and the Council, is not acceptable to the Japanese.

As a result of this interview, it was feared that the discussion and review of the fiscal arrangement by the Council, originally scheduled for this Wednesday, may be postponed until the objections of the Japanese are ironed out.

Observers pointed out that the stand now taken by the Japanese may again prevent the settlement of the outside-road issue which has been "shelved" for the past three years chiefly because the Japanese indicated in 1932 and 1934 that the original agreements worked out by Mr. Fessenden and Mr. O. K. Yui, then Secretary-General of the City Government, were not acceptable.

Districts Marked Off

While the contents of the new Yui-Fessenden tax pact were still unannounced, it was stated unofficially that the extra-Settlement road areas were divided in the agreement into the "Northern" and "Western District."

It was stated that in the "Western" areas the Council is to act as the proxy of the City Government in collecting municipal rates and taxes. Out of the amount collected, the City Government is to pay the Council a certain sum as compensation for utilities and other benefits enjoyed by the residents. A small portion of the tax according to these reports, is to be retained by the City Government.

This tentative agreement, it was stated, was labelled as "unacceptable" by the Japanese on the ground that it did not take into consideration the so-called interests of the local Japanese community.

Mainichi Comments

What is considered by observers as the official view of the local Japanese community was contained in a recent editorial of the Shanghai Mainichi, which stated in part:

"The local Japanese community ....has continuously sought to bring about an amicable settlement of the (outside road) problem, in the desire of creating an ideal residential zone. On one hand, the Chinese have been engaged in the talk of the theory of sovereignty, and the S.M.C. has been hoping for a favorable turn in the situation, paying no attention to the needs of the residents. What is needed is a compromise agreement, which would consider the interests of the Japanese residents . . . Why did the Council, aware of the possibility of a compromise agreement, make such a concession to the Chinese authorities?"

The present Japanese objection, if it achieves the desired result, will be the third time that such a stand has held up the settlement of the outside road question.

In August, 1932, after both the British and American diplomatic representatives had notified the Council of their approval of the modus vivendi, the Japanese Consul-General informed the Council that he was not prepared to accept the arrangement.

His chief objection against the tentative agreement worked out by Mr. Yui and Mr. Fessenden, it appeared, had to do with the police administration in the outside road area.

Blocks Larger Pact

In October, 1934 when the outside road negotiations were resumed, the Japanese Consul-General again refused to accept the Yui-Fessenden agreement on the geographical demarcation and definition of the outside road area.

Although the present agreement only includes provisions on tax collection, it is viewed by the Japanese as a forerunner for a more comprehensive outside road agreement touching on the entire scope of the question.

Observers stated that the Japanese are therefore intent on withholding their support to the initial agreement, thus making it impossible for any further and more comprehensive pact to be formulated.

《字林西报》，1937年4月20日，星期二

发布通告
日本方面
对道路协定
提出异议

吉冈领事
拜会工部局陈述
不予接受

近期达成的协定
遭受挫折

越界筑路问题的
全面解决
现已受到损害

当地日本人提出的反对意见，其性质类似于他们在1932年和1934年提出的反对意见，这可能再次阻碍越界筑路问题的早日解决。

昨日，日本领事吉冈先生（N. Yoshioka）拜会上海公共租界工部局总办费信惇先生（Stirling Fessenden），正式指出，大上海市政府与工部局之间就越界筑路区域税收征管达成的临时协议，是日本方面所不能接受的。这一情况表明了上述担忧。

由于此次会谈，人们担心工部局原定于本周三进行的对该财政安排的讨论和审议，可能会推迟至日本方面的异议得到解决之后。

观察人士指出，日本方面目前采取的立场可能再次阻碍越界筑路问题的解决。该问题在过去三年中主要因日本方面在1932年和1934年表示无法接受由费信惇先生和时任市政府秘书长俞鸿钧先生（O. K. Yui）拟定的原始协议而一直被“搁置”。

划定区域

虽然新的俞鸿钧-费信惇税收协定的具体内容尚未公布，但据非官方消息透露，该协议将越界筑路区域划分为“北区”和“西区”。

据悉，在“西区”，工部局将作为市政府的代理方征收市政捐税。在所征款项中，市政府将向工部局支付一定金额，作为对居民享受公用事业及其他利益的补偿。据报道，税款的一小部分将由市政府留存。

据悉，这一临时协议被日本方面标榜为“不可接受”，理由是该协议未考虑所谓当地日侨社区的利益。

《每日新闻》评论

上海《每日新闻》（Shanghai Mainichi）最近的一篇社论包含了观察人士视为当地日侨社区官方观点的内容，部分摘录如下：

“当地日侨社区……一直寻求达成（越界筑路）问题的友好解决方案，以期创建一个理想的居住区。一方面，中国人一直在空谈主权理论，而上海公共租界工部局（S.M.C.）则希望局势出现有利转折，忽视了居民的需求。现在需要的是一项妥协协议，该协议应考虑到日侨居民的利益……既然工部局知晓达成妥协协议的可能性，为何还要向中国当局做出如此让步？”

如果此次日本的反对意见达到了预期效果，这将是第三次因采取此类立场而阻碍越界筑路问题的解决。

1932年8月，在英国和美国外交代表均通知工部局批准该项临时安排（modus vivendi）后，日本总领事却告知工部局，他准备不接受该安排。

看来，他对俞鸿钧先生和费信惇先生拟定的临时协议的主要反对意见，涉及越界筑路区域的警务管理问题。

阻碍更大范围的协定

1934年10月，当越界筑路谈判恢复时，日本总领事再次拒绝接受俞鸿钧-费信惇关于越界筑路区域地理划界和定义的协议。

尽管目前的协议仅包含税收征管的条款，但日本方面将其视为涵盖整个问题范围的更全面的越界筑路协定的前奏。

观察人士称，因此日本方面决心不支持这项初步协议，从而使制定任何进一步且更全面的协定成为不可能。

THE SHANGHAI SUNDAY TIMES, APRIL 18, 1937

Local Japanese Opposed To
Proposed “Roads” Pact

Nippon Journal Refers To “Abrupt Signing” Of
Tentative Agreement Without Consultation Of
Their Desires; Previous Discussion Recalled

Objection to the “abrupt signing” of a provisional accord on house taxes in the extension areas was voiced in its editorial columns yesterday by the Shanghai “Mainichi.”
Mr. H. E. Arnhold, former Chairman of the Shanghai Municipal Council, announced on Thursday, at the ratepayers’ meeting, the conclusion of an agreement between the Council and the Shanghai City Government on the previous day.
“Although the nature of the accord has not been revealed,” the journal said, “we understand that it provides for the collection of the house taxes by the City Government, while a certain percentage of the receipts will be turned over to the S.M.C., in consideration of its investments in the Extra-Settlement areas and for the facilities it gives these areas.”
There is no doubt, said the daily, that “under the present circumstances,” the Council will approve of the accord.
The extension roads made their appearance, according to the “Mainichi,” in 1927, almost simultaneously with the establishment of the Nationalist Government in Nanking.

Negotiations Started
“With the general improvement in the internal situation, the Chinese authorities shortly afterwards began negotiations for the return of these areas to Chinese jurisdiction. “Negotiations in this matter,” said the journal, “have been in progress between the S.M.C. and the City Government ever since the outbreak of the Manchurian incident.
“The local Japanese community, many of whose members reside in the Western and Northern extension areas, has continuously sought to bring about an amicable settlement of the problem, in the desire of creating an ideal residential zone.
“On the other hand,” the journal asserted, “the Chinese authorities have been engaged in idle talks on the theory of sovereignty, ignoring the actual state of affairs, and the S.M.C. has been hoping for a favourable turn in the situation, paying no attention to the needs of the residents.

“Compromise Needed”
“What is needed is a compromise agreement, which would consider the interests of the Japanese residents, as well as of the S.M.C. and the City Government.”
The journal suggested that such a compromise would have been arranged, if not for the aggravated state of Sino-Japanese relations and the departure of the Japanese officials directly concerned with the matter.
The “Mainichi” concluded its editorial with a query:
“Why did the Municipal Council, aware of the possibility of a compromise agreement among the Japanese residents, the City Government and the S.M.C., make such a concession to the Chinese authorities?”

《上海星期泰晤士报》，1937年4月18日

当地日本人反对
拟议的“道路”协定

《日本日报》提及在未征询其意愿的情况下
“突然签署”临时协议；回顾此前的讨论

上海《每日新闻》在其昨日的社论栏目中，对在扩展区域房屋税临时协定“突然签署”一事表达了反对意见。
上海公共租界工部局前主席安诺德先生（H. E. Arnhold）于周四在纳税人会议上宣布，工部局与上海市政府已于前一天达成一项协议。
该报刊称：“虽然协定的性质尚未披露，但我们获悉，协定规定由市政府征收房屋税，同时考虑到工部局在越界筑路区域的投资以及为该区域提供的设施，所得收入的一定百分比将移交给上海公共租界工部局（S.M.C.）。”
该日报称，毫无疑问，“在目前情况下”，工部局将批准该协定。
据《每日新闻》称，扩展道路的出现是在1927年，几乎与南京国民政府的建立同时。

谈判开始

“随着内部局势的总体改善，中国当局不久后便开始就收回这些区域归中国管辖进行谈判。”该报刊称，“自‘满洲事变’爆发以来，上海公共租界工部局与市政府之间一直就此事项进行谈判。
“当地日侨社区，其许多成员居住在西部和北部扩展区域，一直寻求达成该问题的友好解决方案，以期创建一个理想的居住区。
“另一方面，”该报刊断言，“中国当局一直忙于空谈主权理论，无视实际事态，而上海公共租界工部局则希望局势出现有利转折，忽视了居民的需求。

“需要妥协”

“所需要的是一项妥协协议，该协议应考虑到日侨居民、上海公共租界工部局以及市政府的利益。”
该报刊建议，如果不是因为中日关系恶化以及直接负责此事的日本官员离任，本可以达成此类妥协。
《每日新闻》以一个问题结束了其社论：
“既然工部局知晓日侨居民、市政府和上海公共租界工部局之间有可能达成妥协协议，为何还要向中国当局做出如此让步？”

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Tuesday, April 13, 1937

Pact On Outside
Road Tax System
Initialed Here

Mayor Yui, Fessenden
Conclude Agreement
On Rate Payment

ACCORD TO AVOID
SECOND “SIEGE”

City Government Lauds
Spirit Of Council
In Negotiations

An agreement embodying the tentative arrangement for collection of municipal rates in the outside-Settlement road areas was initialed this morning by Acting Mayor O. K. Yui of the Municipality of Greater Shanghai and Mr. Sterling Fessenden, secretary-general of the Shanghai Municipal Council, at the City Government building.

Contents of the agreement, which is expected to prevent a repetition of drastic action such as that taken by the Council against the “Stupid Valley Village” residents last month, however, were not disclosed this morning.

Interviewed by the Shanghai Evening Post at noon, Acting Mayor Yui expressed deep appreciation of the spirit of the Council in arriving at the agreement. The question about tax collection on the extra-Settlement road areas should not be further delayed, he stated. In concluding the agreement, Acting Mayor Yui continued, the City Government was guided by the principle of protecting the Chinese sovereign rights and at the same time, the principle of fairplay.

The agreement concerning the tentative arrangements for tax collection may eventually pave the way to a complete agreement for administration of the outside-settlement roads, he hoped.

Negotiations on the arrangements for tax collection in the outside-Settlement road areas were started immediately following the settlement of the Council siege of “Stupid Valley Village,” the block of three-story foreign-style houses bordering Bubbling Well, Tifeng and Yu Yuen Roads. It is generally believed that the arrangements embodied in the agreement initialed this morning were in substance similar to the arrangements reached to solve the siege. Under that scheme, the residents pay the 12 per cent municipal rates to the City Government in technical recognition of the Chinese sovereignty over the area while, the City Government turns over the receipts, partly or wholly, to the Council as a “compensation” for the public utility facilities enjoyed by the residents.

《上海晚邮报及信使报》，1937年4月13日，星期二

关于越界筑路
税收制度的协定
在此草签

俞鸿钧市长、费信惇
就捐税缴纳
达成协议

协定旨在避免
第二次“围困”事件

市政府赞扬
工部局在谈判中的
精神

今天上午，大上海市政府代市长俞鸿钧（O. K. Yui）与上海公共租界工部局总办斯特林·费信惇（Sterling Fessenden）在市政府大楼，就在越界筑路区域征收市政捐税的临时安排签署了初步协定（草签）。

然而，今天上午并未披露该协定的具体内容。预计该协定将防止重演上月工部局对“愚园路村”（Stupid Valley Village）居民采取的激烈行动。

俞鸿钧代市长中午在接受《上海晚邮报》采访时，对工部局在达成协议过程中表现出的精神表示深切赞赏。他表示，越界筑路区域的税收征管问题不应再拖延。俞鸿钧代市长接着说，在达成该协议时，市政府遵循的原则是保护中国主权，同时也遵循公平原则。

他希望，有关税收征管临时安排的协议最终可能为全面管理越界筑路道路铺平道路。

关于越界筑路区域税收征管安排的谈判，是在工部局解除对“愚园路村”的围困后立即开始的。“愚园路村”是指毗邻静安寺路（Bubbling Well Road）、地丰路（Tifeng Road）和愚园路（Yu Yuen Road）的一片三层西式住宅街区。人们普遍认为，今天上午草签的协议中所体现的安排，在实质上与为解决围困事件而达成的安排相似。根据该方案，居民向市政府缴纳12%的市政捐税，这在技术上承认了中国对该区域的主权，同时，市政府将全部或部分收入移交给工部局，作为对居民享受的公用事业设施的“补偿”。

THE CHINA PRESS, FRIDAY, APRIL 9, 1937

Talks Opened
Anew Over
Outside Roads

Yui Meets Fessenden
In Following Up Re-
cent Tax Accord

1ST DISCUSSIONS
SINCE 1934

General Principles Are
Believed Gone Over
Yesterday

Foreshadowing an early settle-
ment of the controversial extra-
Settlement road question, the first
discussion during the past two years
to solve the problem was held yes-
terday between Mr. O. K. Yui, acting
Mayor of Greater Shanghai, and
Mr. Stirling Fessenden, Secretary
General of the Shanghai Municipal
Council.

Although the result of the meet-
ing, following the usual practice of
the two negotiators during the past
several years, was not revealed to
the press, it is understood that a
discussion on general principles
took place.

The tacit understanding on various
points achieved during yesterday's
conversation is to be studied in
detail by both parties. Another
meeting is likely to take place
some time next week when the dis-
cussion will be resumed.

Tax Issue Settled

Yesterday's conference between
Mr. Yui and Mr. Fessenden follow-
ed the understanding achieved last
month when the tax siege on a
block of houses in the Yu Yuen and
Tifeng Roads district was settled.

A meeting between Mr. Yui and
Mr. Fessenden was originally sche-
duled to take place during the
week of March 22. As a result of
the appointment of General Wu
Te-chen, former Greater Shanghai
Mayor, to his new Kwangtung
Chairmanship post, the meeting
was postponed.

The conference yesterday, re-
opening a question which had been
deadlocked for some five years, was
the first discussion of the problem
between the two veteran negotiators
since late 1934.

At that time, after protracted
talks, the tentative agreement
reached between Mr. Yui and Mr.
Fessenden was nullified as a result
of the staunch opposition of the
Japanese Consul-General. Since then
the question had been shelved until
the Tifeng Road tax war, which
again thrust the outside roads ques-
tion into the news and political
forefront.

Negotiators Reticent

While neither party was willing
yesterday to discuss the scope of
the talk and the possible points to
be included in the agreement, ob-
servers believe that the settlement
of the outside roads issue devolves
on the following major points:

1. The definition of the term
"extra-Settlement road." This
point will include a geographical
demarcation of the section of ter-
ritory to which the agreement
would apply.

2. The financial and revenue pro-
blem. On this problem, a settlement
would naturally include the dis-
posal of tax collected from the
tenants and the authority which
will collect such tax.

3. The organization of the police
force which will be responsible for
policing the extra-Settlement road
district. If such a separate police
organization is found to be neces-
sary, the question on the personnel,
maintenance and power would
have to be discussed and settled.

4. Public utility. The charges of
telephone, power, light, gas and
water in this new district will form
another question which is likely to
be included in the talks and the
agreement.

S.1.

《字林西报》，1937年4月9日，星期五

关于越界筑路问题
重启谈判

俞鸿钧会见费信惇
以跟进近期达成的税收协定

自1934年以来的
首次讨论

据悉双方昨日已就
一般原则进行磋商

预示着备受争议的越界筑路问题即将早日解决，过去两年来为解决该问题而举行的首次讨论于昨日在大上海代理市长俞鸿钧先生与上海工部局总董费信惇（Stirling Fessenden）先生之间进行。

尽管按照过去几年两位谈判代表的惯例，会议结果未向新闻界透露，但据悉双方就一般原则进行了讨论。

昨日会谈中在各要点上达成的默契将由双方详细研究。另一次会议可能于下周某个时间举行，届时将恢复讨论。

税收问题已解决

俞先生与费先生昨日的会议，是继上月就愚园路和地丰路（Difeng Road）地区一批房屋的税收围困事件达成谅解之后进行的。

俞先生与费先生的会议原定于3月22日那一周举行。由于前大上海市长吴铁城将军被任命为新的广东省主席职务，会议得以推迟。

昨日的会议重新开启了一个僵持约五年的问题，这是自1934年底以来两位资深谈判代表之间就该问题进行的首次讨论。

当时，经过漫长的谈判，俞先生与费先生达成的临时协议因日本总领事的坚决反对而无效。此后，该问题一直被搁置，直到地丰路税收战再次将越界筑路问题推至新闻和政治的前沿。

谈判代表保持沉默

虽然双方昨日均不愿讨论谈话的范围以及协议中可能包含的要点，但观察家认为，越界筑路问题的解决取决于以下几个主要方面：

1. “越界筑路”一词的定义。这一点将包括对协议适用领土部分的地理划界。

2. 财政和收入问题。在此问题上，解决方案自然包括对向租户征收的税款的处理，以及由哪个机构负责征收此类税款。

3. 负责越界筑路地区治安的警察部队的组织。如果认为有必要建立这样一个独立的警察组织，则必须讨论并解决有关人员、维持费用和权力的问题。

4. 公用事业。在这个新区域内，电话、电力、照明、煤气和水的费用将成为另一个可能被纳入会谈和协议的问题。

S.I.

THE CHINA PRESS, FRIDAY, MARCH 19, 1937.

Whole Extra
Roads Issue
To Forefront

Western District Clash
Results In Plan To
Renew Parleys

YUI, FESSENDEN
MEET NEXT WEEK

Meanwhile, Both Offi-
cials Busy Preparing
Their Arguments

By WOO KYATANG
With the Tifeng Road tax impasse finally settled, Shanghai residents yesterday turned their attention toward the knotty extra-Settlement road question, which is scheduled to be re-opened for discussion after a deadlock of nearly five years as a result of the Yui-Fessenden understanding Wednesday.
The first preliminary meeting to discuss a fiscal arrangement on the outside road areas, THE CHINA PRESS learned, is scheduled between Mr. Stirling Fessenden, Secretary-General of the S.M.C., and Mr. O. K. Yui, Secretary-General of the City Government, early next week, possibly Monday.
At the first meeting, the two officials, who have been negotiating this same question off and on for the past five years, will try to outline a general plan of approaching the problem, was learned.
When the scope and purpose of the talks are arrived at by Mr. Fessenden and Mr. Yui, the two will then proceed to discuss the method of the settlement.
Both Officials Busy
Meantime, both officials were yesterday busy preparing their cases for the first meeting next week.
Although it was impossible to learn exactly what will be discussed, the writer was given to understand that possibly the first thing the two negotiators will do is to re-examine the modus vivendi they reached in 1932 and in the spring of 1934.
It was pointed out to THE CHINA PRESS that the two might proceed on the general outline of the previous modus vivendi. On the other hand, it was further stated, Mr. Fessenden and Mr. Yui might change the entire method of approachment, and devise a new plan.
The contents of the 1932 and 1934 modus vivendi were never revealed to the press and it was impossible yesterday to learn the main points contained therein.
Those who closely followed the outside road question, however, recalled yesterday that in July, 1932 preliminary steps were taken by Council authorities to open negotiations in the complicated problem. Nearly two years later, on June 4, 1934, a proposed arrangement, which for the lack of a better name, was described as modus vivendi, was agreed upon by the City Government and the Council.

One of the conditions under which the discussion was carried out was that any agreement reached would be first subject to the approval of the National Government and the various foreign diplomatic representatives concerned.
The modus vivendi thus agreed upon was limited to a general statement of principles which could be applied practically. These included matters concerning police control and administration, taxation and finance, maintenance and repair of roads, operation of public utilities, health and other similar problems.
Details regarding the actual execution of these problems were left for later discussion and adjustment. Also, another important problem regarding the actual demarcation and definition of extra-Settlement areas to which the modus vivendi should apply was also left for subsequent talks.
The Council, at that time, was willing to approve the agreement in the form substantially similar to the one advanced. But it was deemed appropriate to submit the draft agreement for the sanction of the Consular Body.
In August, 1932, local representatives of the American and British Governments informed the Council that the proposal had received the approval of their principals.
Japanese Disagrees
At the end of August that year, the Japanese Consul-General informed the Council authorities that he could not agree to the modus vivendi as it then stood. His chief objection, it was pointed out, had to do with the method of police administration in the extra-Settlement road areas.
In order to work out a compromise on the disputed point, discussion was resumed from the summer of 1932 until October 1933. No definite method of solution, however, was reached.
The question was not settled until the spring of 1934 when, after another series of negotiations, an agreement was reached regarding the numerical strength, composition and the personnel of the special joint police force.
Meantime, discussion proceeded regarding the definition of the area known as "extra-Settlement," and the territory in which the modus vivendi should become operative.
Various proposals were discussed and in October, 1934, City Government authorities submitted a plan for marking off a strip of territory of stated depth on each side of the outside roads and including in addition certain Council property situated outside of the Settlement.
Again Objects
The Japanese Consul-General again put forth his objection, explaining that he could not accept the Chinese plan.
As a result of these setbacks, the entire outside road question was deadlocked. Negotiations were conducted sporadically, but no definite headway was made.
Chinese circles here yesterday hoped that as a result of the understanding for evolving a fiscal arrangement on the outside roads problem, Mr. Yui and Mr. Fessenden will be able to pick up the tangled threads of their former talks and bring about a lasting arrangement on the long-standing question.

（印：SPECIAL BRANCH / B / 9 MAR 1937 / SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE）

《字林西报》，1937年3月19日，星期五。

整个越界筑路问题
被推至前沿

西区冲突导致
计划重启谈判

俞、费二人
将于下周会晤

与此同时，两位官员
正忙于准备各自的论据

作者：WOO KYATANG（音译）

随着地丰路税收僵局最终得到解决，上海居民昨日将注意力转向了棘手的越界筑路问题。鉴于周三俞鸿钧与费信惇达成的谅解，这一僵持了近五年的问题计划重新开放讨论。
据《字林西报》获悉，讨论越界筑路地区财政安排的第一次预备会议定于下周初（可能是星期一）在上海工部局秘书长费信惇先生与市政府秘书长俞鸿钧先生之间举行。
据悉，在第一次会议上，这两位在过去五年中断断续续就同一问题进行谈判的官员，将试图勾勒出解决问题的一般计划。
当费先生和俞先生确定了谈话的范围和目的后，两人将进而讨论解决方法。
两位官员事务繁忙
与此同时，两位官员昨日正忙于为下周的第一次会议准备各自的说辞。
虽然无法确切得知将讨论什么内容，但笔者获悉，两位谈判代表可能做的第一件事是重新审查他们在1932年和1934年春季达成的临时协定（modus vivendi）。
有人向《字林西报》指出，两人可能会以前述临时协定的一般大纲为基础进行。另一方面，还有人表示，费先生和俞先生可能会改变整个处理方法，并制定一个新计划。
1932年和1934年临时协定的内容从未向新闻界披露，昨日也无法得知其中包含的主要要点。
然而，那些密切关注越界筑路问题的人昨日回忆说，1932年7月，工部局当局采取了初步步骤，就这一复杂问题开启谈判。近两年后的1934年6月4日，市政府和工部局同意了一项拟议的安排，由于缺乏更好的名称，该安排被描述为临时协定。

进行讨论的条件之一是，达成的任何协议须首先获得国民政府和相关各国外交代表的批准。
因此达成的临时协定仅限于可实际适用的一般原则声明。其中包括有关警察管制和行政、税收和财政、道路维护和修理、公用事业运营、卫生及其他类似问题的事项。
关于这些问题的实际执行细节留待以后讨论和调整。此外，另一个关于临时协定应适用的“越界”区域的实际划界和定义的重要问题也留待后续会谈解决。
当时，工部局愿意批准实质上与所提方案相似的协议。但认为将协议草案提交领事团批准是适当的。
1932年8月，美国和英国政府的当地代表通知工部局，该提案已得到其本国政府的批准。
日本方面不同意
同年8月底，日本总领事通知工部局当局，他不能同意当时的临时协定。据指出，他的主要反对意见涉及越界筑路地区的警察管理方法。
为了就争议点达成妥协，讨论从1932年夏天一直持续到1933年10月。然而，并未达成明确的解决方法。
直到1934年春天，经过另一系列谈判，才就特别联合警察部队的人数、组成和人员达成协议，从而解决了这一问题。
与此同时，关于被称为“越界”区域的定义以及临时协定应生效的领土范围的讨论也在进行。
讨论了各种提案，1934年10月，市政府当局提交了一项计划，建议在越界道路两侧划定一定深度的地带，并包括位于租界之外的某些工部局财产。
再次提出反对
日本总领事再次提出反对，解释说他不能接受中方的计划。
由于这些挫折，整个越界筑路问题陷入僵局。谈判零星进行，但未取得明确进展。
在沪华人圈子昨日希望，鉴于就越界筑路问题制定财政安排的谅解，俞先生和费先生能够理清之前谈判的乱麻，并就这一长期存在的问题达成持久的安排。

（印：特务处 / B / 1937年3月9日 / 上海公共租界工部局警务处）

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Thursday, March 18, 1937

Joss-Money Fire
Drives Out SMC

“Stupid Valley” Folk
Free As Barricades
Removed From Area

“Enrich yourself with the joss-money and haunt us no more!” This statement, usually murmured by Chinese worshippers to get rid of haunting spirits, was exactly what the Shanghai Municipal Council received when it removed the barricades from the Yu Yuen, Tifeng and Bubbling Well Road exists of “Stupid Valley” village after a siege of the houses for one week in the “tax war.”

Fire Kindled
Right after the Public Works Department coolies had removed the barricades on the Yu Yuen Road main entrance of the half block of three-story, foreign-style

houses, some playful tenants started a bon-fire with joss-money. The gesture implies the time-honored statement and is meant as a bad omen for the Council, from the chairman of the city governing body down to the $4 a month coolie.
The barricades were removed shortly after 4 o’clock yesterday afternoon. The order for the removal was issued by Mr. Stirling Fessenden, secretary-general of the Council, at 3.45 p.m. following agreement with Mr. C. K. Yui, secretary-general of the City Government on the following points:

Sum Guaranteed

1. That the Council undertakes to remove the barricades.
2. That the City Government In consideration of the above fact, guarantees a sum of money equivalent to the rates of the current quarter ending March 31, 1937, as a compensation for utility services and other amenities enjoyed by the tenants.
3. That the City Government to proceed at once to collect “rates” due from the tenants.
4. That after the money is collected, it will be kept in trust by the City Government.
5. That the City Government and the Council enter into negotiations with a view to reaching a fiscal arrangement regarding the tax question of the outside roads.
6. That when such a fiscal arrangement is reached, the money kept in trust by the City Government will be disposed of accordingly.
7. That in the event of a failure to reach a fiscal arrangement, the funds collected by the City Government will be turned over to the Council as a compensation for utility service and other amenities furnished to the tenants.

（印：SPECIAL BRANCH 19 MAR. 1937 SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE）

《上海晚邮报与美商信使报》，1937年3月18日，星期四

纸钱之火
逼退工部局

“愚谷”居民自由了
路障从该地区移除

“拿着纸钱发财吧，别再纠缠我们！”这句话通常是中国信徒为了驱除缠人的鬼魂而低声念诵的，而这正是上海工部局在“税收战”中对“愚谷”村的一批房屋围困一周后，移除愚园路、地丰路和静安寺路（Bubbling Well Road）出口处的路障时所得到的回应。

点燃篝火
就在工务部苦力移除了半街区三层西式洋房在愚园路主入口处的路障后，一些调皮的租户立即用纸钱生起了一堆篝火。这一举动暗示了那句古老的话语，意在给工部局带来坏兆头，从该市政机构的主席到月薪4美元的苦力无一幸免。
路障于昨日下午4点后不久被移除。移除命令由工部局秘书长费信惇先生于下午3点45分发出，此前他与市政府秘书长俞鸿钧先生就以下几点达成了协议：

保证款项

1. 工部局承诺移除路障。
2. 市政府考虑到上述事实，保证提供一笔相当于截至1937年3月31日的当前季度捐税金额的款项，作为对租户享受的公用服务和其他便利设施的补偿。
3. 市政府立即着手向租户收取欠缴的“捐税”。
4. 款项收取后，将由市政府代为保管。
5. 市政府和工部局进入谈判，以期就越界筑路的税收问题达成财政安排。
6. 一旦达成此类财政安排，由市政府代管的款项将据此处理。
7. 如果未能达成财政安排，市政府收取的资金将移交给工部局，作为对提供给租户的公用服务和其他便利设施的补偿。

（印：特务处 1937年3月19日 上海公共租界工部局警务处）

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Thursday, March 18, 1937

Banker Yui
SOMETHING FOR NOTHING is what all of us would like to get. But eating one's cake and having it too is proverbially impossible, and in spite of all the uproar over the "Stupid Valley" affair it seems throughout to have been generally agreed that no one should be permitted to dodge payment of taxes in all quarters by the accident of an ambiguous geographic location.
That is virtually the only point on which there has been general agreement. The Council seems finally to have passed the ball straight into the waiting arms of Mr. O. K. Yui of the Municipality of Greater Shanghai, and the handing-over of tax collections on his part appears to be dependent upon a settlement of the long outstanding Outside Roads controversy.
If this state of affairs results either in a prompt settlement or an announcement as to just what is holding up such settlement, it will be all to the good. Meanwhile we presume the Municipality of Greater Shanghai is as trustworthy a banker as any, and better than some, though we don't know what provision is being made for payment of interest on deposits and it would help to have specific information about withdrawal privileges. There is something reassuring about Mr. Yui's initials, anyway.

《上海晚邮报与水星报》，1937年3月18日，星期四

银行家余（Yui）
不劳而获是我们所有人都想得到的。但是，鱼与熊掌不可兼得，这是一句众所周知的谚语，尽管围绕“愚谷”事件闹得沸沸扬扬，但似乎普遍达成共识：任何人都不应因地理位置界定模糊这一偶然因素，而被允许逃避各方的纳税义务。
这实际上是唯一达成普遍共识的一点。工部局似乎最终将此事直接推给了大上海市政府的余（O. K. Yui）先生手中，而他方面移交税款征收权一事，似乎取决于长期悬而未决的越界筑路争议的解决。
如果这种局面能促成迅速解决，或者至少公布究竟是何原因阻碍了此类解决，那将是好事一桩。与此同时，我们推测大上海市政府作为银行家的可信度不亚于任何机构，甚至优于某些机构，尽管我们不知道对存款利息支付有何规定，若能获得关于提款特权的具体信息将有所帮助。无论如何，余先生的姓名首字母（O.K.）确实令人感到些许宽慰。
